agent_notes: KJV counts this superscription as verse 0 and starts at 68:1 with our verse 2; every later KJV number is one lower than the Hebrew number. I translate the Hebrew verse as it stands.

תָּנִיף 'you shake out' is rendered from נוּף; Ibn Ezra glosses it 'water abundantly', Metzudat Zion 'pour, melt'. STEPBible 'spread abroad' is corrected to 'shake out' to keep the image of rain flung from a hand.

חַיָּתְךָ: STEPBible 'community'. The KJV 'congregation' follows Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion, who cite 2 Sam 23:11 (חַיָּה as a band). The Hebrew is the ordinary word for 'living creature/animal'; the literal layer says 'your living-band' to hold both. Rashi's second reading ('his beast') is recorded in the note.

הַמְבַשְּׂרוֹת is feminine plural participle with the article: women heralds. KJV 'those that published it' erases the gender; the Targum and Ibn Ezra's 'their songs' read it in light of Exod 15 and 1 Sam 18:6. The reading about victory-song women is my own, unsourced.

Revised after review: the claim that the divine title stands 'in the same line of the psalm' is removed. The irony between 'kings of armies' and 'YHWH of armies' is now given as my own observation about a title known from elsewhere in the Bible (e.g. 1 Sam 17:45), not as something this line says. Ibn Ezra and Malbim read the kings as 'kings of the hosts of the nations'. Gloss for נְוַת corrected from STEPBible 'beautiful woman' to 'the dweller of': נָוֶה is a dwelling or pasture, here the female inhabitant (Metzudat Zion reads 'dwelling'). The dramatic layer now continues the packet's previous verse (v12: the Lord speaks a word, the women send it out).

agent_notes: The most disputed verse of the window. שְׁפַתָּיִם is a dual of uncertain meaning: 'hearth stones/cooking-pot rims' (Radak, Ibn Ezra, Metzudat Zion via Ezek 24:3), 'boundaries' (Rashi, YLT), 'sheepfolds' (ASV), 'saddlebags' (STEPBible). Revised after review: Gen 49:14 and Judg 5:16 have the related form מִשְׁפְּתַיִם (mishpetayim), not the same word; that parallel is only an argument for a related meaning. I kept 'the two saddlebags' in the literal layer as one defensible reading. Who is addressed and what is covered in silver and gold are not settled; I did not decide. The Ps 89:51 parallel for the inverted order is Meiri's, not Radak's; Radak says only that the attribute stands in place of the thing described and the order is reversed. The remark about a plated dove statue is my own unsourced guess.

agent_notes: בָּהּ (feminine 'in it') has no clear antecedent: the land (Ibn Ezra), Jerusalem (Radak), the dove of v14. תַּשְׁלֵג is read as a jussive/indicative 'it snows' (hiphil with impersonal subject); Radak notes it may be transitive. 'Zalmon' as a mountain near Shechem (Judg 9:48) is likely; Ibn Ezra puts it east of the Jordan. STEPBible tags it as Ebal, which I did not follow in the text, only in the commentary. Rashi and Metzudat Zion link the name to צַלְמָוֶת 'deep darkness', a possible wordplay, and I flagged it as such without asserting it.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses 'O mountain of' (vocative); the Hebrew construct הַר־אֱלֹהִים is more naturally a nominal clause 'a mountain of God is Bashan'. I corrected the glosses to the plain construct. The reading of אֱלֹהִים as an intensifier ('a mighty mountain') versus 'of God' is noted in the commentary. גַּבְנֻנִּים is a hapax, from גַּב 'back, hump' (Rashi quoting Ezek 16:24, Radak), translated 'many-peaked' or 'humped'.

תְּרַצְּדוּן is a hapax. Rashi cites Menachem for 'dance' (cf. רקד) and Moshe HaDarshan for an Arabic root 'lie in wait'; Metzudat Zion and Meiri take 'dance'. I follow the hostile-glance sense ('eye with envy', as ASV, YLT, BBE) in the dramatic layer and the literal layer reads 'watch with envy', and say so; the KJV 'leap' follows the 'dance' reading. Not a certain gloss; the lexica (BDB, HALOT) are themselves unsure.

שִׁנְאָן is another hapax. Rashi and Radak take it as 'angels' (שִׁנְאַנִּים), Ibn Ezra as 'repetition' (שנה, 'two'), and STEPBible gives 'repetition[s]', which is the root-based reading. I rendered the literal as 'thousands of repetition', which preserves the word as it stands, and left 'angels' to the commentary. The verb is absent in the Hebrew: 'the Lord [is] among them, Sinai in the holiness' is elliptical, and the 'as in Sinai' of KJV and ASV smooths it. I kept the gap in the literal layer.

The famous verse. 'Among humankind' (בָּאָדָם) is literal; KJV 'for men' and Eph 4:8 'gave gifts to men' follow the Targum/Peshitta tradition of a reversed sense ('gave'), not the Hebrew, which says 'took'. Rashi reads the one who goes up as Moses taking the Torah; the Targum agrees; Radak and Meiri read it as a lament; I presented these options and did not choose. I translated שָׁבִיתָ שֶּׁבִי as 'you took captivity captive' in the literal layer to keep the cognate accusative, and 'you led captives away' in the dramatic. The sense of the final clause (God dwelling among the rebellious, or the rebellious dwelling with God) is ambiguous: לִשְׁכֹּן has no stated subject.

יַעֲמָס־לָנוּ lacks an object, which Radak and Metzudat David supply as 'his blessings/benefits' (hence KJV 'loadeth us with benefits'). ASV and YLT read it as 'bears [our burden]'. The Hebrew idiom is 'bears a load for us'. In the dramatic layer I kept the ambiguity. Malbim reads the object as 'our salvation', which is grammatically also possible.

לַמָּוֶת תּוֹצָאוֹת: 'issues' (KJV) is archaic English for 'ways out, exits' (cf. Prov 4:23). Whether 'to death' means 'ways out from death' (rescue) or 'exits leading to death' (Rashi, Radak, Malbim: the variety of deaths God inflicts) is open; the verse and the next, which says what God does to enemies, favour the latter, but the parallel 'God of saving acts' favours the first. I kept the literal ambiguity ('escapes to death') and, in the commentary, named both readings. The reading of יְהוִה אֲדֹנָי as 'the Lord YHWH' is correct; the Masoretic vocalisation of the first word gives יֱהוִה, i.e. read Elohim, which is the reason for the 'GOD' in some English versions.

history.note: [consider] Credit 'escape from death' to ASV (and BBE, 'ways out of death'), and say that YLT keeps 'outgoings'. (PS.68.21 YLT: 'And Jehovah Lord hath the outgoings of death'; ASV: 'escape from death')

agent_notes: Radak, Rashi, and Meiri take 'hair-scalp' as a figure; Rashi reads 'hairy' as Esau (Gen 27:11), which I mention but treat as a rabbinic reading. The expression קָדְקֹד שֵׂעָר 'crown of hair' is literal. מִתְהַלֵּךְ בַּאֲשָׁמָיו is a habitual participle: 'one who goes about in his guilts', a person who keeps walking in guilt.

אָשִׁיב has no stated object, and 'my people' (KJV, Webster, in italics) is an addition. The sense could be 'bring back the enemy' (Ibn Ezra, Malbim, Radak) or 'bring back my people' (Rashi, Meiri, Metzudat David). I kept the object out of the literal layer and only suggested in the dramatic one that the voice speaks of return, from the two extremes of height and depth, without naming who returns. The two limits (Bashan, the sea) suggest a merism.

Textual and grammatical difficulties. תִּמְחַץ 'it may smash': Rashi reads 'break through' the blood (cf. Judg 5:26). Radak and, in Ibn Ezra, R. Yehudah read it as an inverted form of חמץ 'redden' (cf. Isa 63:1, quoted by Meiri). I followed the Masoretic text, 'smash'. A modern emendation reads תִּרְחַץ 'bathe'; that is outside the packet and not from any commentator here, and I mention it only as such. The verb יִמְחַץ is in v22, which the commentary now says. מִנֵּהוּ 'its portion': Rashi and Metzudat Zion link it to מָן 'ration' (Dan 1:10, Exod 16:15); Ibn Ezra offers alternatives. 'Dogs' as scavengers is the common reading (1 Kgs 21:19, 22:38). The sentence about the gods of Bashan was deleted.

agent_notes: מִקְדָּשֶׁיךָ is plural with a yod; the Masoretic text may well intend the plural of majesty. בָּעֲרָבוֹת is a real split: STEPBible 'in the clouds', KJV 'upon the heavens', YLT/ASV/BBE 'deserts/deserts-way'. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri take it as a name for heaven; Malbim and the 'steppes' reading fit 'Arabah' and the wilderness march of v. 8.
